newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Cocoa - Erratic weather unlikely to hit Ivory crop.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa - Erratic weather unlikely to hit Ivory crop.

text.p: Topsy-turvy weather in Ivory Coast, characterised by unseasonal rainy and dry spells, is unlikely to have a dramatic effect on the 1996/97 cocoa crop as the bulk of it is already well established, crop analysts say.
"Fundamentally, I think that there is nothing to worry about as the bulk of the crop it well established. There will be no dramatic effect", one local analyst told Reuters on Wednesday.
He said some young fruits might suffer slightly from the late arrival of this year's short rainy season.

But he added that if the rain lasted longer into the season than usual it could be beneficial, as it would soften the drying effect of the harmattan wind from the north, which can seriously affect cherelle (early pod) setting.
"I'm not worried at all" he said.

Robert Fish of the UK forecaster PCR Ltd shared this view. "It's not going to make a huge difference for the overall total of the crop because your setting at this time is pretty light anyway," he said in London this week.
Data from Ivory Coast's national weather station showed rainfall for the first 10 days of November in the following key growing areas plus the commercial capital Abidjan were -
Daloa 0 mm, Gagnoa 25.8 mm, Abidjan 15.4 mm, San Pedro 18.4 mm, and Tabou 19.2 mm
Forecasters were caught off guard last season by the late shaping of the record 1.2-million tonne crop.

Pod counters scouting the Ivorian cocoa fields reported unusually low levels of soil moisture at the end of October. Early drought affects the survival of the tail of the crop, usually the last 100,000 tonnes, and may reduce the bean size.
Previous forecasts for the total 1996/97 crop range from 900,000 to 950,000 tonnes.
The local analyst explained that the weather pattern in Ivory Coast has been erratic since July.
Usually there is a small dry season in July and August, but this year there was lots of rain.
"In July and August, there was almost double the normal level of rain. According to our records it was a 20-year record," said the analyst.
The short rainy season normally arrives between September and October, but this year conditions were very dry. Weather data showed less than 50 percent of average October rains fell in Ivory Coast.
The dry season usually begins at the start of November. Abidjan in particular has experienced heavy rain since the start of this week.
